summary: Defines an echo function for the connectionless network layer protocol, ISO 8473. Two mechanisms are introduced, the first as an interim solution for the Internet community. It was replaced by RFC 1574 and RFC 1575.

plainLanguage.summary: Shouting "hello?" down a hallway to see if someone is there. This gives a way to do that on the ISO kind of network.

subtitle: A diagnostic mechanism for testing the connectionless network layer.

tldr.problem: The OSI connectionless network layer (ISO 8473) lacks a simple way to test whether network paths are functioning, making it difficult to debug gateway and link failures.
tldr.mechanism: An echo function allows a system to send an echo-request packet and receive a copy back, similar to ping. The RFC defines two mechanisms: a backward-compatible short-term approach using NSAP selectors, and a long-term approach using new PDU types.
tldr.outcome: This interim standard was later superseded by RFC 1574 and RFC 1575, which defined the official ISO approach.

today: RFC 1574 and RFC 1575 superseded this interim specification with the official ISO echo mechanism.

sections.title: Why Echo Matters for Network Testing
sections.content:
The ISO 8473 connectionless network layer protocol (CLNP) handles datagram transmission and relaying in an OSI internet. However, the real-world networks carrying CLNP packets are imperfect: gateways fail, links go down, and packets are lost. Debugging these failures is difficult because network management protocols that could diagnose problems themselves depend on working packet delivery, creating a chicken-and-egg problem.

An echo function solves this by providing a lightweight diagnostic mechanism at the network layer. A system can send an echo-request packet to a remote machine and expect an echo-reply coming back. If the reply arrives, the path works; if not, something is broken. Importantly, the echo path must use the same code path as normal data, so it fails and succeeds in unison with regular traffic—making it a reliable diagnostic tool.

This memo defines echo using two approaches: a backward-compatible short-term version and a long-term version suitable for future ISO standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Network paths can break, but we need a simple way to check if they're working without relying on complicated management systems. Echoing is like a ping: send a test packet, get an answer back.

sections.title: How the Echo Function Works
sections.content:
The echo function is conceptually simple. A sending system builds an echo-request PDU (Protocol Data Unit) with the remote system as the destination. This request travels through the network like any normal data packet, following the same routing and processing rules. When it reaches the destination system, it is delivered to an echo-request entity—a function that processes echo requests.

The echo-request entity then constructs an echo-reply PDU and sends it back to the original sender. The entire echo-request PDU, including its header and data, is encapsulated inside the echo-reply packet's data portion. This way, when the sender receives the reply, it can examine fields like the original packet's lifetime to determine how long the round trip took and whether the packet was modified.

The key design constraints are simplicity (so all systems implement it), code-path identity (the echo path must match normal data path exactly), and backward compatibility (existing systems should not break when echo packets pass through).
sections.plainLanguage: Send a message to a distant computer. When it arrives, that computer wraps the message inside a new message sent back to you, so you can verify the round trip worked.

sections.title: Two Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC defines a short-term approach for immediate adoption and a long-term approach for future ISO standards.

Short-term approach: Echo packets are built using normal ISO 8473 Data (DT) PDU construction. The trick is in the NSAP address selectors. The echo-request uses a reserved selector value (decimal 30 by default) in the destination address to identify it as an echo-request. The source address uses a different selector value (decimal 31) to identify the echo-reply return path. To systems that do not implement echo, these packets look like perfectly ordinary data packets and are routed normally. Only systems that recognize the special selector values understand that these are echo packets and generate replies. This approach is maximally backward-compatible: old routers switch echo packets like any other data, and old endpoints simply ignore them.

Long-term approach: Two new PDU types are defined, ERQ (echo-request, type code 30) and ERP (echo-reply, type code 31). These are identical to DT PDUs except for the type code. This approach is not backward-compatible with existing ISO 8473 but may be adopted by ISO as an addendum to the standard.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to do this. The quick way hides echo messages inside ordinary packets using special addresses—old systems won't recognize them as special but will deliver them anyway. The proper way creates official new packet types, but old systems might not know what to do with them.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Several rules govern how echo packets are handled. First, the same discard rules applied to normal DT PDUs apply to echo packets—if the lifetime field expires, the packet is discarded.

Second, error report handling differs slightly. If an echo-request is discarded and has the error report flag set, an error report is sent back to the original sender. If an echo-reply is discarded, the error report goes to the source address of the echo-reply (typically the echo-request entity itself).

Third, the lifetime field in both echo-request and echo-reply should use normal data values—the RFC does not attempt to define special lifetime handling for echo packets.

Most PDU options (flags that modify behavior) from the echo-request are copied into the echo-reply, with two exceptions. The record route option is copied but reset to allow the echo-reply to record a complete path. The source route option is explicitly not copied, because source-routed echo requests can cause packet loops. Similarly, while the RFC allows priority values in echo headers, it cautions against using high priority, as normal data priority should apply.

Finally, multiple processes on a single machine may send echo-requests simultaneously. How a system correlates replies to requests among multiple processes is a local implementation matter not defined by this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: When handling echo packets, follow the normal rules: discard if they're too old, report errors properly, and don't try to force special priority or routing that normal packets wouldn't use.
